newsitem.title: GERMANY: Allianz sees higher sales, profit in 97.
newsitem.headline: Allianz sees higher sales, profit in 97.

text.p: German insurer Allianz AG Holding said on Wednesday it expected its sales and earnings to improve in 1997, with underwriting earnings expected to show a profit for the first time since 1990.
Chairman Henning Schulte-Noelle said in the text of a speech to be delivered to a news conference that business so far in 1997 allowed a cautious prognosis for the full year.

"We want to break even in the Allianz Group's underwriting result in 1997 as well as achieve moderate double digit profit growth and make further progress in the growth markets of Central and Eastern Europe and Asia," he said.
Non-underwriting earnings should also continue to improve, given favourable conditions on capital markets, the group added in its annual report.
Allianz had already reported a rise of 10.7 percent to 2.24 billion marks ($1.3 billion) in 1996 net profit, having narrowed its underwriting loss to 148 million marks in 1996.
Schulte-Noelle also said the group aimed for a return on equity this year that further approached its goal of 15 percent.
Schulte-Noelle said Allianz aimed for 15 percent return on equity, up from 11.2 percent after tax in 1996, by the year 2000 and also wanted to achieve a higher earnings per share result this year.
Allianz's earnings per share rose to 9.25 marks from 8.72 marks in 1996.
In its annual report, Allianz said its premiums would grow by about 11 percent to 83 billion marks this year, mainly due to the inclusion of new units.

The first time inclusion of the Vereinte health insurance group would raise premiums by 8.3 billion marks and there would be an extra 1.2 billion marks from the full 12-month inclusion of the Berner and Hermes units.

At the same time, the shedding of Deutsche Krankenversicherung would cause premiums to drop by 3.4 billion marks. Premiums income would rise by a good six billion marks as a result of structural changes.
Excluding these changes, premiums would rise three percent, or around two billion marks.
